1
INTERESTS OF AMICI CURIAE

If there is anything this Court’s near century of
Second Amendment jurisprudence teaches, it is that
“the government cannot completely ban an arm in
common use for lawful purposes.”  Hanson v. District
of Columbia , 120 F.4th 223, 256 (D.C. Cir. 2024)
(Walker, J., dissenting).  Yet numerous lower courts
have not heeded this lesson.  They have held that legislators may ban outright weapons that they “determine[] [a]re unusually dangerous  because of their
characteristics”—regardless of whether those weapons are in common use for lawful purposes—so long as
the legislature deigns to preserve “alternatives for
self-defense and other lawful purposes.”  Nat’l Ass’n
for Gun Rights v. Lamont, 153 F.4th 213, 222, 232-33
(2d Cir. 2025).  And they have held unprotected those
firearms that are, in the court’s estimation, “ill-suited
and disproportionate to the need for self -defense.”
Bianchi v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438, 441 (4th Cir. 2024)
(en banc); accord Bevis v. City of Naperville , 85 F.4th
1175, 1193-95 (7th Cir. 2023).  The result?  A fundamental right that is subject to legislative caprice and
judicial speculation about what the right-holder really
“needs.”

Tennessee and Kansas, along with Alabama,
Alaska, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana,
Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri,
Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Dakota,
Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina,
South Dakota, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, and Wyoming, have a significant interest in ensuring that the
Second Amendment receives the full protection this

2
Court’s precedents require.  Amici States’ citizens are
among the millions of Americans who own AR-15 platform and other similar semiautomatic rifles for numerous lawful purposes —including for hunting, for
sport, and for defense of self and others.  The AR -15
platform rifle is popular for many reasons, not the
least of which are its reliability and relatively low recoil, which make it an excellent target gun.  Amici
States are also home to lawful businesses that manufacture and sell these semiautomatic rifl es across the
country.  Decisions that narrow the scope of the Second Amendment—and affirm the outright ban of the
AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles —
leave constitutional rights dependent on geography
and invite States (and the federal governm ent) to enforce restrictions on the Second Amendment that this
Court’s precedents do not permit.

Amici States cherish the freedom our Nation’s federalist structure provides States “to devise solutions
to social problems that suit local needs and values.”
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742, 785 (2010)
(plurality opinion).  Amici States also, as a general
matter, assiduously defend the rights of state legislatures to address policy issues as they see fit.  “But the
enshrinement of constitutional rights necessarily
takes certain policy choices off the table,” District of
Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 636 (2008)—including a wholesale ban on semiautomatic rifles in common use for lawful purposes.

3
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

 Respondents banned the AR-15 platform rifle—the
most popular rifle in the country—and countless similar rifles.  “Tens of millions of Americans” own at least
one of the approximately twenty million AR-15 platform rifles in circulation in the United States.  Snope
v. Brown , 145 S. Ct. 1534, 1535 (2025) (Thomas, J.,
dissenting from the denial of certiorari).  And the
“overwhelming majority” of Americans who possess
“them do so for lawful purposes, including self-defense
and target shooting.”  Id. (internal quotation marks
omitted).  Indeed, the reported criminal use of any rifle
is limited compared to other weapons, including handguns.

Those facts should have made these cases easy.
This Court has already determined that the Second
and Fourteenth Amendments protect the possession
and use of “arms ‘in common use’” “for lawful purposes
like self-defense.”  See Heller, 554 U.S. at 624-25; accord N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen, 597
U.S. 1, 21 (2022); McDonald, 561 U.S. at 780 (plurality
opinion).  The banned semiautomatic rifles plainly fall
within this category of protected arms.

The courts below concluded otherwise based on a
cramped view of the Second Amendment that is inconsistent with this Court’s precedent.  This Court should
honor the Second Amendment’s guarantee and hold
that it does not allow a categorical ban on AR-15 platform or other semiautomatic rifles in common use for
lawful purposes.

4
ARGUMENT

I. The Second and Fourteenth Amendments
Protect Arms Commonly Used for Lawful
Purposes.

The Second Amendment commands that “the right
of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.”  U.S. Const. amend. II.  As its “very text” reveals, Heller, 554 U.S. at 592, “[t]he Amendment ‘was
not intended to lay down a novel principle but rather
codified a right inherited from our English ancestors’”—the “individual right to keep and bear arms,”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 20 (quoting Heller, 554 U.S. at 595,
599).

“[T]he founding generation cherished the Second
Amendment.”  Wolford v. Lopez, 146 S. Ct. 2032, 2042
(2026).  “Founding-era legal commentators confirmed
the importance of the right to early Americans,” with
St. George Tucker “describ[ing] the right to keep and
bear arms as ‘the true palladium of liberty’ and explain[ing] that prohi bitions on the right would place
liberty ‘on the brink of destruction.’”  McDonald , 561
U.S. at 769.  As Justice Story later put it in his Commentaries, the right to keep and bear arms “offer[ed]
a strong moral check against the usurpation and arbitrary power of rulers; and [would] generally, even if
these are unsuccessful in the first instance, enable the
people to resist and triumph over them.”  3 J. Story,
Commentaries on the Constitution of the United
States § 1890 (1833).

5
The Second Amendment, of course, “originally applied only to the Federal Government.”  McDonald,
561 U.S. at 754.  But “[t]he constitutional Amendments adopted in the aftermath of the Civil War fundamentally altered our country’s federal system,” including by rendering “the Second Amendment right
. . . fully applicable to the States.”  Id. at 750, 754.  Indeed, “Congress’s desire to enable the newly freed
slaves to defend themselves against former Confederates” in the aftermath of the Civil War “helped inspire
the passage of the Fourteenth Amendment,” which in
turn “secured the right to bear arms again st interference by the States.”  United States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S.
680, 690 (2024).

Despite this historical pedigree and the Second
Amendment’s textual command, “[f]or many years,
the Second Amendment lay dormant as a sort of second son among constitutional rights.”  Bianchi , 111
F.4th at 493 (Richardson, J., dissenting).  But then
came Heller and McDonald.  Heller revived the Second
Amendment by holding that it “protects a personal
right to keep and bear arms for lawful purposes, most
notably for self-defense within the home.”  McDonald,
561 U.S. at 780 (plurality opinion).  And McDonald
confirmed that this “Second Amendment right is fully
applicable to the States.”  Id. at 750.

Still, lower courts “resist[ed] this Court’s decisions.”  Silvester v. Becerra, 583 U.S. 1139 (2018)
(Thomas, J., dissenting from the denial of certiorari).
They applied exceedingly “deferential” standards of
review in challenges to firearms restrictions and

6
generally failed “to afford the Second Amendment the
respect due an enumerated constitutional right.”  Id.

Enter Bruen.  There, this Court clarified the two -
part test courts must apply to determine whether a
modern firearm law violates the Second Amendment.
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 17.

At step one, a challenger must establish that “the
Second Amendment’s plain text covers [his] conduct.”
Id.1  This initial “inquiry entails three subsidiary
questions.”  Wolford, 146 S. Ct. at 2043.  First, “does
the law apply to ‘the people’—which is to say, to ‘all
members of the political community’?”  Id . (quoting
Heller, 554 U.S. at 580).  Second, does the law “concern
any form of ‘Arms,’ i.e., any weapon customarily used
for offensive or defensive purposes?”  Id. (citing Heller,
554 U.S. at 584).  Third, does it “place any restrictions
on either the ‘keeping’ (i.e., possession) or the ‘bearing’
(i.e., carrying) of arms?”  Id. (citing Bruen, 597 U.S. at
32-33) (alterations adopted) .  If the answer to those
questions is yes, then the Second Amendment’s plain
text covers the challenger’s conduct, and the Constitution “presumptively protects” it.  Bruen , 597 U.S. at
24.

At step two, the government must present evidence from the “Nation’s historical tradition of firearm
regulation” to “justify its regulation.”  Id.  When evaluating these historical analogues, courts should

1 If the plaintiff brings a facial constitutional challenge, the plaintiff must show that “no set of circumstances exists under which
the Act would be valid.”  Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 693 (quoting United
States v. Salerno, 481 U.S. 739, 745 (1987)).

7
consider: “(1) the number of jurisdictions in which the
historical restrictions were adopted, (2) the extent to
which the historical restrictions were well -accepted,
whether expressly or tacitly, and (3) whether the historical restrictions are ‘relevantly similar’ to the modern challenged law.”  Ass’n of N.J. Rifle & Pistol Clubs,
Inc. v. Att’y Gen. N .J., 183 F.4th 211, 231 (3d Cir.
2026) (en banc) (citing Wolford, 146 S. Ct. at 2044).

The Bruen inquiry “can be difficult.”  Bruen , 597
U.S. at 25  (citation omitted).  It “sometimes requires
resolving threshold questions and making nuanced
judgments about which evidence to consult and how to
interpret it.”  Id.   But as this Court’s precedents explain, certain Second Amendment principles are pellucid.

One such principle governs here: the Second
Amendment protects those weapons “typically possessed by law -abiding citizens for lawful purposes.”
Heller, 554 U.S. at 625; accord Caetano v. Massachusetts, 577 U.S. 411, 420 (2016)  (Alito, J., concurring)
(same).  This protection of “the possession and use of
weapons that are ‘in common use at the time’” follows
from the “historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”  Bruen , 597
U.S. at 21 (quoting Heller, 554 U.S. at 627).  The takeaway is simple: “[W]eapons in common use today for
self-defense and other lawful purposes remain fully
protected.”  Snope, 145 S. Ct. at 1536 (Thomas, J., dissenting from the denial of certiorari) (internal quotation marks omitted); see McDonald, 561 U.S. at 780
(plurality opinion) (“[T]he Second Amendment protects a personal right to keep and bear arms for lawful

8
purposes, most notably for self- defense within the
home.”); see also Heller, 554 U.S. at 599 (explaining
that “most” Americans at the founding “undoubtedly
thought” the Second Amendment was “important for
self-defense and hunting”).

II. Semiautomatic Rifles Are Commonly Used
for Lawful Purposes.

The semiautomatic rifles Respondents banned “fit
neatly within th[is] category of protected arms.”
Snope, 145 S. Ct. at 1536 (Thomas, J., dissenting from
the denial of certiorari).  AR-15 platform rifles are undoubtedly in common use.  And, along with other modern sporting rifles, they are “overwhelming[ly]” used
“for lawful purposes” like target practice, hunting, and
self-defense.  Id. (internal quotation marks omitted);
see infra at 12-13.  In fact, rifles (semiautomatic and
manual-action alike) appear in violent crime statistics
dramatically less often than other commonly possessed weapons, including handguns.

A. Millions of Americans own AR-15 platform
and comparable semiautomatic rifles.

 Semiautomatic rifles have been a popular choice
for firearm owners for more than a century.  They were
“first introduced in 1885,” seven years before the creation of the first semiautomatic pistol.  Nat’l Rifle
Ass’n Inst. for Legis. Action, “Assault Weapons” and
“Large” Magazines, https://perma.cc/A3A4 -GYB6.
Eighteen years later, semiautomatic rifles reached
public markets and quickly became “a runaway commercial success.”  Heller v. District of Columbia , 670

9
F.3d 1244, 1287 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting) (Heller II ).  Manufacturers like Winchester,
Remington, Standard Arms, and Browning Arms
rushed to create their own versions with varying calibers, magazine sizes, and grips (including pistol
grips).  Id.  These “rifles were designed and marketed
primarily for use as hunting rifles,” although there
was “a small ancillary market among law enforcement
officers.”  Id.

 The AR-15 platform rifle is a semiautomatic rifle.
It “was first developed as a military rifle in the 1950s
by ArmaLite.”  Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 517 (Richardson,
J., dissenting).2  In the 1960s, Colt acquired the patent
and “created a semiautomatic version” that it marketed and sold “to civilians and law enforcement.”  Id.
“Colt’s patent expired in 1977, and other companies
began mass producing similar models for civilian use.”
Id. at 517-18.

Although “[t]he AR-15 semiautomatic rifle has the
outward appearance of an M16 military service rifle,”
it “lacks the latter’s critical feature of fully automatic
fire.”  Stephen P. Halbrook, America’s Rifle: The Case
for the AR -15 14 (2022) (Halbrook); see Staples v.
United States, 511 U.S. 600, 603 (1994) (describing the
differences between the AR -15 and the military’s M -
16 rifle).  “The AR -15-type semiautomatic has never
been issued as a service rifle to U.S. soldiers,” nor are
semiautomatic rifles “issued as standard service rifles

2 “AR” is a reference to the Armalite brand; it does not stand for
“assault rifle.”  See Mock v. Garland , 75 F.4th 563, 569 n.7 (5th
Cir. 2023).

10
to any army in the world.”  Halbrook 16.  The superficial similarity in appearance between the AR-15 platform rifle and standard service rifles simply reflects
that certain ergonomic and design features translate
well to both military and civilian use.

Since the AR-15 platform rifle entered the market,
the popularity of semiautomatic rifles among the
American citizenry has only grown.  Consider the
sheer number of semiautomatic rifles in circulation.
Since 1990, over 32 million modern sporting rifles
(roughly 1 for every 11 Americans) have been produced in or imported into the United States.  Nat’l
Shooting Sports Found., Firearms Production in the
U.S., https://perma.cc/YAW8-EYTR.  Some estimates
suggest “around 24 million AR -[1]5s and similar
sports weapons remain in circulation—a figure that is
surpassed only by the number of registered handgun
owners within the United States.”  Ass’n of N.J. Rifle
& Pistol Clubs, Inc., 183 F.4th at 241.  And that may
be a conservative estimate.  “As of 2021,” other sources
suggest, “there are at least twenty -eight million AR -
style semiautomatic rifles in circulation,” with
“[r]oughly 2.8 million of those weapons enter[ing] the
market in 2020 alone.”  Bianchi , 111 F.4th at 518
(Richardson, J., dissenting).  To put that into perspective, that means “there are more AR-style rifles in the
civilian market than there are Ford F -Series pickup
trucks on the road—the most popular truck in America.”  Id.

Ownership trends tell the same story.  In 2021,
approximately one third of adults in the United
States, about 81.4 million people, reported owning a

11
firearm.  William English, 2021 National Firearms
Survey: Updated Analysis Including Types of Firearms Owned , Georgetown McDonough Sch. of Bus.
Rsch. Paper No. 4109494, at 1 (May 13, 2022),
https://perma.cc/E8H9-N6RZ (English Survey).  Of
those gun owners, between 16 and 24.6 million own an
AR-15 platform or similar rifle.  Id. at 20 (“30.2% of
gun owners, about 24.6 million people, have owned an
AR-15 or similarly styled rifle”); see also Poll of current
gun owners , at 1, Wash. Post -Ipsos (2022),
https://perma.cc/YSJ5-STNS (Wash. Post -Ipsos Survey); Emily Guskin et al., Why do Americans own AR-
15s?, Wash. Post (Mar. 27, 2023),
https://perma.cc/U6M6-QRDG (indicating based on
Wash. Post -Ipsos Survey that roughly 16 million
Americans “own an AR -15-style rifle”).  In 2022, the
ATF determined that these “AR -15-type rifle[s]” are
“one of the most popular firearms in the United
States.”  Definition of ‘Frame or Receiver’ and Identification of Firearms, 87 Fed. Reg. 24652, 24652 (Apr. 26,
2022) (to be codified at 27 C.F.R. pts. 447, 478, and
479).  And just last year, this Court unanimously recognized that “[t]he AR -15 is the most popular rifle in
the country,” “widely legal[,] and bought by many ordinary consumers.”  Smith & Wesson Brands, Inc.  v.
Estados Unidos Mexicanos, 605 U.S. 280, 297 (2025);
see Snope, 145 S. Ct. at 1536 (Thomas, J., dissenting
from the denial of certiorari) (noting that “[t]ens of
millions of Americans own AR-15s”).

Against that backdrop, it is “beyond debate” that
AR-15s and similar rifles meet the requisite “common
use” threshold.  Bianchi , 111 F.4th at 519 (Richardson, J., dissenting) (citation omitted).  “[T]he many

12
millions of [these] semi-automatic rifles in circulation
. . . are plainly in common use.”  Ass’n of N.J. Rifle &
Pistol Clubs, Inc. , 183 F.4th at 242.  And they have
been for decades.  See Heller II, 670 F.3d at 1269 (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting) (“Semi -automatic rifles, like
semi-automatic handguns, have not traditionally been
banned and are in common use by law-abiding citizens
for self-defense in the home, hunting, and other lawful
uses”).  Any conclusion to the contrary blinks reality.

B. The overwhelming majority of AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles are
possessed and used lawfully.

Millions of Americans own AR -15 platform and
similar rifles, and the overwhelming majority use
their rifles for lawful purposes.  Many, following a tradition as old as the Republic, take them to the field to
hunt game.  English Survey, at 33 -34; Wash. Post-Ipsos Survey, at 1.  Indeed, the smaller .223 caliber AR-
15 platform rifle is recognized as a legal caliber for
hunting North America’s whitetail deer in many
States, see, e.g., Kan. Admin. Regs. § 115-4-4(c), while
larger AR -platform rifles can be chambered in .308
Winchester—a longstanding choice for hunting larger
game animals, see Craig Boddington, The .308 Winchester, Boone and Crockett Club (Spring 2014),
https://perma.cc/BCC7-L7RG.  Other Americans use
their AR-15 platform rifles to dispatch predators and
varmints.  Responsive Mgmt. for Outdoor Stewards of
Conservation Found., Proliferation of Hunting With
AR-Platform / Modern Sporting Rifles, at  16 (2023),
https://perma.cc/UL6S-WKGV.  Still others simply enjoy “endless hours of fun on the rifle range.”  Philip

13
Schreier, A Short History of the Semi-Automatic Firearm, America’s First Freedom (June 28, 2022),
https://perma.cc/5CZV-3A8T.  And many owners also
keep their AR-15 platform semiautomatic rifles to defend what matters most: their families, their homes,
and themselves.

The use of rifles for defense, especially home defense, is not new.  For centuries, Americans have used
the rifle as an instrument of self- defense.  Colonists
“habitua[lly]” carried rifles for that purpose.  John Adams, To the Inhabitants of  the Colony of Massachusetts-Bay, Nat’l Archives:  Founders Online (Feb. 6,
1775), https://bit.ly/2SwaXi4.  The rifle later became
“the companion of the pioneer.”  Heller, 554 U.S. at 609
(citation omitted).  And when the law failed to protect
Americans from violence, rifles assumed an especially
important role.  During the struggle over slavery in
“Bloody Kansas,” efforts to disarm “Free -Soilers”
prompted “Senator Charles Sumner, who later played
a leading role in the adoption of the Fourteenth
Amendment, [to] proclaim[] that ‘[n]ever was [the rifle] more needed in just self-defense than now in Kansas.’”  McDonald, 561 U.S. at 770 (third and fourth alterations in original) (quoting The Crime Against Kansas: The Apologies for the Crime: The True Remedy ,
Speech of Hon. Charles Sumner in the Senate of the
United States 64-65 (1856)).  That tradition continued
after the Civil War, when rifles became “particularly
popular among marginalized groups” during the Jim
Crow era.  C.D. Michel & Konstadinos Moros, Restrictions “Our Ancestors Would Never Have Accepted”:
The Historical Case Against Assault Weapon Bans, 24
Wyo. L. Rev. 89, 110-11 (2024).

14

The tradition of using rifles for self- defense continues today among owners of semiautomatic rifles.  In
surveys, the majority of those who own AR -15 platform rifles have said that they keep their rifles for selfdefense.  In the 2022 Washington Post -Ipsos survey,
91% of respondents indicated that one of the reasons
they owned an AR-15-style rifle was to “[p]rotect self,
family and property,” with 65% specifying that this
was a “[m]ajor reason” motivating their ownership.
Wash. Post-Ipsos Survey, at 1.  Professor William English’s 2022 National Firearms Survey is in accord,
with 61.9% of respondents indicating that they owned
an AR-15 platform or similar rifle for “home defense.”
English Survey, at 33-34.

As of 2021, 31.1% of firearm owners reported using a firearm in defense of themselves or their property, with rifles used in 13% of those incidents.  English Survey, at 12, 14.  Stated differently, “[a]ssuming
that defensive uses of firearms are distributed roughly
equally across the years, this suggests at least 1.67
million defensive uses of firearms per year”—with approximately 127,480 of those incidents involving rifles.  Id. at 9, 12.

Tennesseans alone can tell stories about how they
successfully used semiautomatic rifles to protect
themselves and their families.  A Memphis man used
a semiautomatic rifle to shoot two armed robbers who
were “ransack[ing]” his house.  Action News 5, Homeowner shoots, kills 2 burglars with AK -47 (June 1,
2018), https://perma.cc/J47A -PFUV.  Another Memphis man used an AR-15 platform rifle to fend off two

15
robbers at his apartment complex.  Ned Dannenberg,
Prosecutors drop charges against U of M student over
apartment shooting , Action News 5 (Mar. 21, 2019),
https://perma.cc/2T8S-RQNN.  A man in Roan Mountain was able to fend off an armed home-invader using
a .22 caliber rifle after he had been shot and wounded
by a bullet from the home-invader’s gun.  Elizabethton
Star, Man charged in Roan Mountain shooting arraigned in General Sessions Court Monday  (Mar. 9,
2022), https://perma.cc/4DLL-93HW.

Tennessee is not an outlier.  A pregnant woman in
Lithia, Florida, saved the lives of her husband and
daughter by shooting a masked and armed home invader with the family’s AR -15.  CBS Miami, Florida
Woman Uses AR -15 To Defend Family During Home
Invasion (Nov. 5, 2019), https://perma.cc/G778-EWTV.
A bystander in Oswego Township, Illinois, used an
AR-15 platform rifle to stop an ongoing stabbing attack, requiring only the “threat of force” to do so.
Shannon Antinori, AR -15-Wielding Neighbor Speaks
Out, 2 Charged In Stabbing , Patch (Feb. 26, 2018),
https://perma.cc/3RZG-U7NK.  In many instances,
simply brandishing the rifle is enough to scare away a
home invader.  A student in Rochester, New York, did
exactly that, protecting himself and his roommate
from armed intruders mere ly by brandishing his unloaded AR-15 platform rifle.  RIT Students Accosted by
Gunmen in their Home , WHAM (July 10, 2013),
https://perma.cc/E8GC-ZBL7.  A 23 -year-old in Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, used an AR-15 platform rifle to
shoot and kill three armed intruders during a home
invasion.  Associated Press, No charges against Oklahoma man who killed 3  intruders (Apr. 3, 2017),

16
https://perma.cc/N65S-ZTDB.  And during the unrest
of summer 2020, small -business owners used AR -15
platform rifles to deter would -be looters from raiding
their storefronts.  See CBS LA, Santa Monica Owner
Protects His Store With Guns Amid Looting  (June 1,
2020), https://perma.cc/4XSA-HGFS.  The list goes on.

That AR-15 platform and other similar semiautomatic rifles are the weapons of choice for citizens seeking to protect themselves and their families is not surprising.  They are widely recognized as an effective
self-defense weapon.  The U.S. Concealed Carry Association has recommended the use of rifles for homedefense, describing the rifle as having superior “handling, hit probability and accuracy” to other home -defense choices.  Bob Campbell, Best Home- Defense Rifles, U.S. Concealed Carry Ass’n (Oct. 1, 2024),
https://tinyurl.com/b82bddc6; accord Ass’n of N.J.  Rifle & Pistol Clubs, Inc. , 183 F.4th at 241- 42 (recounting district court finding that semiautomatic rifles’
“build and design features, such as their mild recoil,
ergonomics, and accuracy make them ‘a good choice for
self-defense.’”).  And even gun control proponents
agree that “in almost all situati ons ‘shotguns and rifles are much more effective in stopping a [criminal]’”
than other weapons.  Brief for Violence Pol’y Center
and the Police Chiefs from the Cities of L.A., Minneapolis, and Seattle as Amici Curiae Supporting Petitioners, District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570
(2008), 2008 WL 136348, at *30 (alteration in original).

Police departments across the country have
reached the same conclusion.  According to a 2023

17
report from the Department of Justice’s Bureau of Justice Statistics, 94.5% of local police departments have
authorized semiautomatic rifles for on -duty officers.
Sean E. Goodison & Connor Brooks, Bureau of Just .
Stats., U.S. Dep’t of Just ., Local Police Departments,
Procedures, Policies, and Technology, 2020 – Statistical Tables, at 8 tbl. 3 (Nov. 2023),
https://perma.cc/MY5W-3JF3.  As the Chief of Police
and Police Captain of the City of Lawrence, Kansas,
Police Department put it, “patrol rifles are a necessity
in today’s environment where disaster can be averted
or minimized when quick action with the right equipment is taken.”  Memorandum from Tarik Khatib,
Chief of Police, & Anthony Brixius, Police Captain,
Lawrence Police Dep’t, to Tom Markus, City Manager,
re: Campaign Zero (Aug. 10 , 2016), https://tinyurl.com/mr3cew4f.

That millions of Americans choose “to keep and
bear” semiautomatic rifles for lawful purposes is sufficient to confer Second Amendment protection.  Heller,
554 U.S. at 625.  That the majority of those Americans
selected a semiautomatic rifle for self -defense makes
the question even easier.  “[I]ndividual self -defense is
‘the central component ’ of the Second Amendment
right.”  McDonald, 561 U.S. at 767 (quoting Heller, 554
U.S. at 599).  And a weapon lawfully owned by tens of
millions of Americans for that purpose cannot be
banned categorically by States without violating the
Constitution.  See id.; Heller, 554 U.S. at 628-30.

In short, there is no historical analogue in the
framing period or during the early American Republic
for categorically banning a firearm that is so

18
commonly used for lawful purposes.  Respondents’
bans are the equivalent of banning the musket in
1789—the very firearm the American colonists in the
colonial militias brought with them to battle during
the American Revolutionary War.  It would be absurd
to suggest that the First Congress and the States that
ratified the Second Amendment thought that the fundamental right to keep and bear arms would permit
the banning of common muskets.  It didn’t —and it
likewise does not permit the categorical prohibition of
modern firearms in common use for lawful purposes.

C. Relative to handguns and other weapons,
rifles are less often criminally misused.

Most people who own AR -15 platform and other
similar semiautomatic rifles keep and bear them for
lawful purposes.  But not all people do.  Amici States
are no stranger to the criminal misuse of semiautomatic rifles and the tragedy of lives lost due to crim inal violence.  Acknowledging these heartbreaking
tragedies, however, does not answer the constitutional
question presented here.  And although rifles of all
kinds are capable of misuse, the available data belie
any contention that they are a more prevalent instrument of criminal violence than other weapons.

 Where FBI data identify firearm type, rifles (both
semiautomatic and manual -action) are involved in a
small share of violent offenses.  In the past year, the
FBI identified:

• 378 homicides involving rifles, compared to
3,817 involving handguns, 1,229 involving

19
knives or cutting instruments, and 506 involving “[p]ersonal [w]eapons” —that is, “[a] person’s hands, arms, feet, fists, or teeth used as a
weapon,” Fed. Bureau of Investigation, Law Enforcement Officers Killed and Assaulted
(LEOKA) Data Collection: Definitions and Examples (2019), https://ucr.fbi.gov/leoka/
2019/resource-pages/definitions;

• 9,925 aggravated assaults involving rifles, compared to 112,987 involving handguns, 115,553
involving knives or cutting instruments, and
152,682 involving personal weapons;

• 20 rapes involving rifles, compared to 876 involving handguns, 948 involving knives or cutting instruments, and 52,876 involving personal weapons; and

• 1,151 robberies involving rifles , compared to
24,481 involving handguns, 11,660 involving
knives or cutting instruments, and 55,401 involving personal weapons.

Fed. Bureau of Investigation, Crime Data Explorer,
(last visited Sept. 1, 2026), https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/
LATEST/webapp/#/pages/explorer/crime/crime-trend
(1-year statistics).3


3 The FBI separately reports violent offenses involving an unidentified firearm.  But where firearm type is identified, handguns overwhelmingly predominate.

20
The data show that this trend has held true over
time.  Over the last 10 years, the FBI has identified:

• 3,809 homicides involving rifles, compared
to 43,342 involving handguns, 10,787 involving knives or cutting instruments, and
5,439 involving personal weapons;

• 91,927 aggravated assaults involving rifles,
compared to 1,093,789 involving handguns,
897,505 involving knives or cutting instruments, and 1,110,679 involving personal
weapons;

• 174 rapes involving rifles, compared to
9,285 involving handguns, 9,730 involving
knives or cutting instruments, and 509,151
involving personal weapons; and

• 11,632 robberies involving rifles, compared
to 344,040 involving handguns, 107,447 involving knives or cutting instruments, and
415,735 involving personal weapons.

Id. (10-year statistics).

Tennessee’s and Kansas’s experiences match the
national data.  In the last 10 years, the FBI has identified 2,270 Tennessee murders by handgun and 181
by rifle.  Fed. Bureau of Investigation, Crime Data Explorer: Expanded Homicide Data (last visited Sept. 1,
2026), https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/
pages/explorer/crime/shr (Tennessee statistics).  And
the FBI cataloged twice as many murders committed

21
by knives or cutting instruments as by  rifles.  Id.  In
the same time period in Kansas, the FBI identified 492
murders by handgun, 112 murders by knives or cutting instruments, and 32 murders by rifle.  Id. (Kansas
statistics).  The data for Respondents’ States are in accord.  In the last 10 years in Illinois, the FBI has recorded 4,440 murders by handgun compared to 130 by
rifle.  Id. (Illinois statistics).  And in the same time period in Connecticut, the FBI has recorded 178 murders
by handgun and 6 by rifle.  Id. (Connecticut statistics).

The relative paucity of violent crimes involving rifles does not diminish the pain that each of those
crimes inflicts on the victims, their families, and their
communities.  The evidence of relatively limited criminal misuse of rifles of all kinds does, however, bolster
the conclusion that AR -15 platform and similar rifles
are in common use for overwhelmingly lawful purposes—and therefore cannot be banned outright.  After all, this Court already rejected the proposition that
“the problem of handgun violence” permitted “the absolute prohibition of handguns held and used for self -
defense in the home.”  Heller, 554 U.S. at 636.  And
“handguns—not rifles—are used in the vast majority
of murders and other violent crimes that individuals
commit with guns in America.”  See Snope, 145 S. Ct.
at 1534 (Kavanaugh, J., respecting the denial of certiorari) (emphasis added).  If handguns are nevertheless
protected from wholesale prohibition, so too are the
most popular semiautomatic rifles in common use for
lawful purposes.

To be sure, States are not powerless to address the
criminal misuse of firearms within their borders.

22
States remain free to “legislate[] within the parameters of our historical tradition.”  Barnett v. Raoul, 180
F.4th 1035, 1081 (7th Cir. 2026)  (Brennan, C.J., dissenting).  To take just a few examples, States can impose objective shall -issue licensing regimes.  See
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 79-80 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring).
They can prohibit the carrying of arms in “sensitive
places such as schools and government buildings.”  Id.
at 30 (quoting Heller, 554 U.S. at 626).  And they can
disarm individuals who “pose[] a clear threat of physical violence to another.”  Rahimi , 602 U.S. at 698.
“The Constitution leaves [States] a variety of tools for
combating” gun violence.  Heller, 554 U.S. at 636.  But
it takes off the table a wholesale ban of a firearm commonly owned for lawful purposes.

CONCLUSION

 The Court should reverse.
